chapter 01 Representation Self-attention The transformer

chapter 01 · transformer — part 0 of 3

Dimension, features, and the latent space

Attention operates on vectors. This is where the vectors come from — and why a network spends one half of itself raising dimension and the other half lowering it. Get those two moves straight and encoder, decoder, embedding and “latent space” stop being jargon.

In one sentence. Raising dimension makes a problem separable; lowering it makes the solution reusable. An embedding is the second move applied to a vocabulary, and the space it lands in is continuous — which is the whole difference between understanding something and looking it up.

Raising dimension: making the problem easy

The vocabulary first, since the rest of the page leans on it:

Start with the smallest useful case — two inputs, a wide hidden layer, one output. Its first act is to turn a 2-dimensional point into a 10-dimensional one, and in matrix form that is the entire operation:

Which invites an objection: if every new coordinate is just a combination of the old ones, no information has been added. So what is gained? Look at what it does to data that was not separable to begin with:

Another frame of the same lift

Why this is the deeper reason attention works at all. Scoring two tokens with a raw dot product asks a question in the coordinates you were handed. Wq and Wk first move both tokens into a space where the question is easy — the same move, applied to relevance rather than to classification.

Lowering dimension: making the answer reusable

Real networks do not stay wide. Past the first layers the neuron count falls — 512 to 128 to 64 to 32 — while the model gets deeper and more capable:

They do — and the lecture makes that case in four steps, worth following in order because each one takes away something you were allowed to assume.

Step 1 — features you picked yourself. Should a video be recommended? Feed in the numbers you already trust:

Step 2 — same idea, harder output. Eight facial muscle movements decide among eight emotions:

Step 3 — the problem. You never actually receive muscle movements. You receive a photograph:

Step 4 — let the network find them. Put the pixels in and make the middle layer narrow:

Raise to separate, lower to generalise. Those two moves do opposite things on purpose. A wide layer makes the boundary easy to draw; a narrow one forces the network to keep only what transfers. Train on pixels and you memorise photographs; train through eight muscle movements and you can read a face you have never seen.

Features compose, and depth buys abstraction

Nobody hand-names those features in practice. Train a digit classifier and the hidden neurons become feature detectors on their own — strokes, curves, corners:

An earlier frame — before the stroke detectors are drawn

Watch it on a different digit — the same fragments, reassembled:

What the narrow layer is: a latent space

Give that middle layer a name and the vocabulary falls into place. The compressed coordinates are a latent space (潜空间), and projecting an input into it is embedding. For words, the coordinates behave like independent basic meanings:

So an encoder is now describable in one line: tokenize → one-hot → project down into the latent space. The sentence has been placed somewhere in a space organised by meaning. A decoder runs the same road backwards, out of the latent space into a sequence of tokens.

translation, two wayshow
embed first, unify afterChinese and English get separate vocabularies and separate latent spaces, then an algorithm aligns the two spaces
unify first, embed afterboth languages go into one vocabulary and train together, landing in a single shared latent space from the start

Either road ends in the same place — a latent space both languages share — and once you have that, translation is: encode Chinese into a point in that space, decode that point into English. The “code” in encode and decode is the latent representation.

Why it matters that the space is continuous

This is the part that makes the whole construction worth the trouble, and Searle's thought experiment is the sharpest way to see it:

The rule book is a key–value table; a latent space is not. That is the whole distinction. A table answers only what someone wrote into it — meet an input that is not a key and it has nothing. A latent space is continuous: unseen inputs land between known ones, near things they resemble along axes that mean something, and a sensible output can be read off a point nobody put there.

Which is the honest version of the claim that a model “understands”: not that it has inner experience, but that its representation generalises past the examples in a way a lookup table cannot. Whether that deserves the word understanding is exactly what Searle was arguing about, and this page does not settle it — but it does name the mechanism the argument turns on.

Everything so far builds one vector per token, each still embedded in isolation — 苹果 has the same coordinates in “apple pie” and in “Apple released a phone”. Fixing that is what the next part is for: self-attention, where each token's vector is rewritten using the others around it.
